Asturian

[edit]

Verb

[edit]

andare

  1. first/third-person singular pluperfect indicative of andar
  2. first/third-person singular imperfect subjunctive of andar

Italian

[edit]

Alternative forms

[edit]
  • andar (apocopic)
  • andà (Tuscan)
  • annare (Umbrian, Laziale, Romanesco)

Etymology

[edit]

Inherited from Early Medieval Latin andāre, of uncertain origin.

Pronunciation

[edit]
  • IPA(key): /anˈda.re/[1]
  • Audio:(file)
  • Rhymes: -are
  • Hyphenation: an‧dà‧re

Verb

[edit]

andàre (first-person singular present vàdo, first-person singular past historic andài, past participle andàto, first-person singular future andrò, first-person singular subjunctive vàda, second-person singular imperative vài or và', auxiliary èssere) (intransitive)

  1. to go [auxiliary essere]
    andare a casa ― to go home
    andare veloce ― to go fast
  2. (intransitive, impersonal, third person only) to be agreeable (to), to be pleasing (to) (idiomatically, to feel like, to want/like) [with a ‘person with feeling’ and di ‘thing desired’] [auxiliary essere]
    non mi va di ballare ― I don't feel like dancing (literally, “it isn't agreeable to me to dance”)
    mi andrebbe del gelato ― I'd like some ice cream (literally, “it would be agreeable to me of ice cream”)
  3. to attend (school, church regularly) [with a]
    andare a scuola ― to attend school
  4. (auxiliary) used to form the passive voice with a connotation of obligation or prescription
    I documenti vanno firmati.
    The documents have to be signed.
    I bambini vanno accompagnati a scuola dai loro genitori.
    Children must be brought to school by their parents.
  5. to enter, to take on, to experience [with in ‘a condition, emotion, etc.’] [auxiliary essere]
    andare in estasi ― to go into ecstasies
    andare in collera ― to get angry (literally, “go into anger”)
    andare in fallimento ― to go bankrupt (literally, “go into bankruptcy”)

Latin

[edit]

Etymology

[edit]

Possibly from *ambitāre (literally “go around”), frequentative of ambiō. Alternatively, perhaps from an earlier *amnāre < *amlāre < ambulāre (“walk”), or from Celtic root mn- (“to go”) + Latin termination -are. Attested from 801 CE in southern Italy.[1] Presumably suppletive with vādō and īre in various conjugations, as are most of the descendants, and as was the contemporary synonym alāre.

Verb

[edit]

andāre (Early Medieval Latin)

  1. to go

    • andur
  • Italo-Romance:
    • Corsican: andà
      Gallurese: andà
      Sassarese: andà
    • Italian: andare (see there for further descendants)
      Central dialects: annà
    • Neapolitan:
      Tarantino: andare
    • Sicilian: annari (Gallo-italic of Sicily)
  • North Italian:
    • Lombard: andà, nà
    • Ligurian: andâ, anâ
    • Piedmontese: andè
    • Venetan: ndar, nar, nare, ndare
  • Gallo-Romance:
    • Catalan: anar
    • Old Franco-Provençal: annar, anar
      • Franco-Provençal: anâ
    • Old Occitan: annar, anar
      • Occitan: anar
  • Ibero-Romance:
    • Asturian: andar
    • Old Galician-Portuguese: andar (see there for further descendants)
    • Spanish: andar
      • → Gascon: andar
